draft.title: Dating the first arrivals
card: Archaeologists study objects and remains left by people in the past. To find out how old a site is, they use scientific dating methods.
measures a form of carbon left in once-living things, such as charcoal, bone or shell. It shows when that living thing died.
measures energy stored in grains of sand or buried sediment. It shows when the grains were last exposed to sunlight, so it can date the layer an object lay in.

At Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land, dating of the layers of earth that held stone tools and ochre shows people lived there more than 60,000 years ago. This means people have lived in Australia for more than 60,000 years.
draft.remember: Scientific dating of sites like Madjedbebe shows people have lived in Australia for over 60,000 years.

a.q: Why do archaeologists use methods such as radiocarbon dating at ancient sites?
opts: To work out how old a site and its layers are
To tell which people made each tool at a site
To find where buried objects are before digging
To show what language people at a site spoke
a.why: Dating methods measure physical changes in materials, which gives the age of a find or the layer it lay in. They cannot show who made a tool or what language people spoke, because those are not stored in carbon or sand grains.
a.clue: Both methods answer a question about time.

b.q: Dating of sand layers at Madjedbebe showed they were buried more than 60,000 years ago, with stone tools inside them. What does this suggest?
opts: People were living in Australia more than 60,000 years ago
People first reached Australia about 40,000 years ago
People made tools here only after the sand was buried
People in Arnhem Land stopped using stone tools long ago
b.why: Tools found in layers that are over 60,000 years old mean people were there at that time. The 40,000 year figure is too recent, as the tools were in older layers.
b.clue: Tools in a layer must be as old as that layer, or younger.

a.best: To work out how old a site and its layers are

b.best: People were living in Australia more than 60,000 years ago

problems.detail: The clue 'Tools in a layer must be as old as that layer, or younger' points students the wrong way. Saying the tools may be younger than the layer weakens the right answer and makes the distractor 'People made tools here only after the sand was buried' seem plausible. The card teaches that the date of a layer dates what lay in it, and the why says the tools show people were there at that time, so the clue contradicts both. It also uses 'must'.

proposal.title: Dating the first arrivals
card: Archaeologists study objects and remains left by people in the past. To find out how old a site is, they use scientific dating methods.
measures a form of carbon left in once-living things, such as charcoal, bone or shell. It shows when that living thing died.
measures energy stored in grains of sand or buried sediment. It shows when the grains were last in sunlight, which is when they were buried. Objects sealed in that layer are about the same age.

a.q: Why do archaeologists use methods such as radiocarbon dating at ancient sites?
opts: To work out how old a site and its layers are
To tell which people made each tool at a site
To find where buried objects are before digging
To show what language people at a site spoke
a.why: Dating methods measure physical changes in materials, which gives the age of a find or the layer it lay in. They cannot show who made a tool or what language people spoke, because those are not stored in carbon or sand grains.
a.clue: Both methods answer a question about time.

b.q: Dating of sand layers at Madjedbebe showed they were buried more than 60,000 years ago, with stone tools inside them. What does this suggest?
opts: People were living in Australia more than 60,000 years ago
People first reached Australia about 40,000 years ago
People made tools here only after the sand was buried
The sand layers were dated using radiocarbon dating
b.why: Objects sealed in a layer are about the same age as that layer, so the tools show people were there more than 60,000 years ago. The idea that the tools came after the sand was buried is wrong, because the tools were sealed inside it when it was buried. The 40,000 year figure is too recent.
b.clue: What does the age of a layer tell you about the objects sealed in it?
